messages.body_plain:
Hello again. I have a couple of follow up questions.

I would like to perform power analyses on this data to see if I should add more stations or not. I have not done much of this  and it has been a while. Would I use the numbers counted at each station and the resulting variance for this or is there some way to account for the distance component? Also, which software would be good for this? I have used Monitor in the past but assume there are a bunch of R packages now, although I am not well versed in R.

Many thanks for all of the help.

Scott

On Monday, July 29, 2024 at 7:55:59 AM UTC+10 scott Vogt wrote:
> Thank you Eric and Mark, this helps quite a bit.
>
> Yes, I took the course in 2014. If you remember, I was with a Japanese biologist, who is probably one of the few in Japan who can do distance sampling.
>
> Understood that this might not be the end all be all might not be any better than stratifying by region. The stations are systematic and I can stratify by region and have done that and also without stratification. I will try the post-stratification overlap and see what that does. Many thanks for the link to the detailed instructions on that.
>
> Acoustic type surveys would probably be worthwhile but we don't have a budget for that and these surveys are in an urban developed area with lots of backround noise (e.g. fighter jets). It's an interesting situation. You might have heard about brown treesnakes on Guam? A non-native arboreal nocturnal bird eating specialist on a whole island of birds that did not evolve with such a thing. The snake was accidentally transported to Guam during or just after WWII. So the micronesian starling is the only native forest bird left on Guam. It's a cavity nester and this remnant population (it exists in large numbers on other islands in the chain) nests in the buildings in the base housing area where there is snake trapping and base buildings and forages in the forest during the day. We had a project the put out nesting boxes to mounted on power poles that snakes could not access. we'd like to monitor the population and I think distance point counts might be the way to go. This project also did telemetry and survival rates.
>
> Thank you for all of the help!
>
>
> Scott
>
> On Thursday, July 25, 2024 at 4:48:49 PM UTC+10 Eric Rexstad wrote:
> > Greetings Scott; I remember your participation at a workshop in St Andrews some years ago.
> >
> > Understandably, the encounter rate variance will increase because of the station with the large number of detections. Removal of that station from the data set is not a good idea and you guessed.
> >
> > The post-stratification tool you describe can be used if the design of the survey used a systematic design. The challenge associated with a systematic design is that an encounter rate variance formula is employed that assumes random transect placement. Usually that approximation is fine, but under some circumstances (an animal gradient compounded by differing transect lengths) this approximation is poor.
> >
> > The post-stratification technique is not intended to reduce the estimated encounter rate variance; in fact, under many simulated scenarios the technique does not reduce estimated encounter rate variance compared to the usual formula. What I mean is the post-stratification technique is not a panacea; it is intended to address a particular situation.
> >
> > That said, slides 9-12 of the variance estimation lecture in our online materials discussed how to perform post-stratification for point transect surveys
> >
> > https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/lecturepdfs/Ch5/L5-1%20Variance%20Estimation%20for%20Systematic%20Designs.pdf
> >
> > The second portion of the exercise on post-stratification shows that post-stratification does not have the desired effect upon encounter rate variance under "normal" conditions:
> >
> > https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/exercisepdfs/Ch5/E5.1%20systematic%20variance%20estimation%20SOLUTION.pdf
> >
> > Hope that is helpful.

> >
> > Hello,
> >
> > I am a biologist working on an Air Force base on Guam. We recently did point count surveys on base for a locally listed bird, Micronesian starling. We have 65 count stations using variable circular plot (5 minute counts) methodology.. For 64 stations our detections were 0-11birds. Sixteen stations had zero. However one station had 28 birds. They are not a flocking species but will live in family groups, but this one spot  has a couple of trees, that appear to be a popular "hang out" spot.
> >
> > So, this station has caused really wide confidence intervals. With transect lines one can post stratify with overlapping lines to reduce variance. Can we do something similar with point counts? would dropping this station from the analyses be a viable option (I'm guessing the answer is no but had to ask)?
> >
> > Any advice would be greatly appreciated.
> >
> > Scott

messages.body_plain:
Scott

Your question is a bit vague in that you haven't indicated what it is you wish to calculate the power of. Difference between two habitats, difference between two points in time, trends over time, ...

Fundamentally the power of any statistical procedure includes the precision of the density or abundance estimates. Given a specified target precision (measured by coefficient of variation), number of point transects needed to achieve the target precision is approximated by some simple formulas found in Section 2.4.2.1 of Buckland et al. (2015):

There is a function to perform these calculations in the dssd package on CRAN, but they are easy to compute with a calculator.

Other work that is relevant to the subject can be found in these references:
Clark RG (2016) Statistical Efficiency in Distance Sampling. PLoS ONE 11(3): e0149298. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0149298. Archived R package  https://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/Archive/distance.sample.size/
Andersen, E. M., & Steidl, R. J. (2020). Power to detect trends in abundance within a distance sampling framework. Journal of Applied Ecology, 57(2), 344–353. https://doi.org/10.1111/1365-2664.13529

 <https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0149298>
Statistical Efficiency in Distance Sampling <https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0149298>
doi.org <http://doi.org>

This might also be relevant to your question

Evaluation of data collected by Guam Division of Aquatic and Wildlife Resources during population establishment and monitoring of ko’ko’ (Hypotaenidia owstoni) on Rota, Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, and wildlife monitoring datasets on Cocos Island and Guam. Hawai‘i Cooperative Studies Unit Technical Report HCSU-109. University of Hawai‘i at Hilo. 101 pages. http://hdl.handle.net/10790/5391

messages.body_plain:
Scott

The causal chain between number of transects and power to detect trends over time has many links. Number of transects influences the precision of the resulting density estimates as I showed from Section 2.4.2.1 in my previous email.

How does precision influence power to detect temporal trend? That is more complex as other factors (magnitude of change per unit time, whether change is linear or exponential, Type I error rate, length of survey time series) as well as precision also come into play. To answer your question, you will need to provide information on all these aspects.

As a proof of concept, I constructed a tool to explore how effort required can be approximated for line transect surveys given input on the components I described in the previous paragraph. Other caveats and underlying literature are included in the description of the tool. The tool is something I developed for teaching purposes, use at your own risk, but it gives you an idea of the steps involved in answering your question.

Paula

There is misunderstanding about the use of the dht2 function that appears occasionally. The use of this function is restricted to situations where you have a stratified design and want an overall estimate across strata treated in a particular manner. In your situation, where you are considering strata to be the years of repeated surveys, I would be surprised if there was biological interest in the sum of estimates across years.

If my supposition is correct, then you need not use dht2 thereby circumventing whatever hassles you are having. If you are using Region.Label as year, then the output coming from the ds  function will provide you with year-specific estimates, which I think is what you require.

If I have misunderstood your question, please provide additional details.

Scott

As you know, with line transects, effort is measured in meters or kilometers while with points, effort is measured in number of stations.

I think you can still use the tool I showed when thinking about points, you simply have to re-define the encounter rate you provide. The tool labels encounter rate as number of detections per kilometer; for your purposes encounter rate is number of birds per station.

Fooling around with the tool, I imagined that your encounter rate was 1.8 birds per station and that you would conduct annual surveys for 10 years, during which time the population would change by 50%. The tool calculates that a CV of 0.143 (precision) would be required to detect that change with power of 0.8. Effort (number of stations required) would be 82 in this situation.

The first step in diagnosing the problem is determining which model generates the error. From your partial output, I'm guessing the ~distance+VegClass model caused the problem. To be sure, run that model alone (without the loop).

messages.body_plain:
Samundra

There are many reasons that could give rise to the observed distribution of perpendicular distances you show. Most common reasons for this distribution are a) evasive movement on the part of the animals or b) distribution of animals available to be detected is lower at small distances from the transect.  Cause b) is often associated with transects placed along features known to the animals; such as tracks.

If you have eliminated these possible causes, only then can you consider other explanations. Transects need not necessarily be straight, but perpendicular distances do need to be recorded to the transect; this is most easily accomplished with straight transects.

Even if it is correct that compass bearings are at fault, I do not know how you would correct the recorded data. Corrections you might make would also be based upon supposition; thereby introducing new uncertainty into the data.

If the cause of the problem is (b) above, then left truncation is not the remedy. See the short note published by Marques (2016) in response to a paper that employed left truncation in an ungulate survey:
Marques, T. A. (2016). A comment on Horcajada-Sánchez and Barja (2015): A cautionary tale about left truncation and density gradients in distance sampling. Annales Zoologici Fennici, 53(1/2), 52–54.

I would second what Eric suggested. My experience with ungulate distance sampling surveys (white-tailed deer, Odocoileus virginianus). The histogram you shared would be typical for surveys conducted from roads (because deer avoid the areas near roads) or because the survey was conducted on foot and deer were able to detect observers first and move away from the transect line. In the first case (roads as transect), you need independent data to model the distribution of deer relative to the transect (Marques et al. 2013 https://doi.org/10.1007/s10260-012-0223-2). In the second case (deer avoid observers) I'm not sure what you do except modify your data collection methods.

Duane Diefenbach
